prompt: A team calls a two-host KVM/libvirt platform highly available. Both hosts share one rack, power feed, management switch and writable NFS export. Twelve VMs request 4 vCPU and 16 GiB each; each host has 32 logical CPUs and 128 GiB, but no failure reserve is calculated. CPU model and QEMU machine type float with host defaults. VM disks are qcow2 overlays whose backing-file paths were copied manually. Templates retain machine-id, SSH host keys and cloud-init cache. A production VM and its clone share a UUID, MAC and writable UEFI NVRAM file. Operators use root over an unencrypted remote libvirt channel. A planned live migration runs while the destination thin pool is nearly full; the target lacks CPU features exposed by the source. The command reports completion, but the VM reboots, takes the old IP, cloud-init skips per-instance work, and the application never becomes ready. Diagnose the evidence, give the immediate safe recovery, redesign provisioning and migration, calculate the minimum host-level reserve question, and explain what HA can and cannot mean here.
directAnswer: The platform has two compute nodes but one physical, management and storage failure domain, so host count does not establish high availability. Requested fleet capacity is 48 vCPU and 192 GiB before hypervisor, page cache, emulator, migration and failure reserve. One surviving host offers only 32 logical CPUs and 128 GiB raw, so memory alone makes full host-loss recovery impossible. Floating CPU and machine types make compatibility depend on current hosts and versions. Manually copied qcow2 overlays can point to missing or wrong bases. Reused UUID, MAC, NVRAM, machine-id, SSH keys and cloud-init cache collapse domain, network, firmware and guest identity. Root and plaintext management make the control plane unsafe. Near-full destination storage and incompatible CPU should have failed preflight. Tool completion proves only command state; reboot, duplicate IP, skipped initialization and failed application readiness disprove service recovery. Stop further migrations and duplicate guests, isolate the clone and duplicate network identity, preserve source/destination/domain/image/migration/audit evidence, establish one authoritative VM and disk chain, protect storage from concurrent writers, restore the last known-good domain on a compatible host with capacity, then validate guest identity, filesystems, network, cloud-init, application state and user flow. Redesign with immutable host/emulator/machine/CPU capability inventory; schema-validated unique domain identity; explicit image format and verified backing chain; sanitized sealed templates; per-instance metadata/NVRAM/MAC; least-privilege encrypted management; capacity and failure-domain placement; migration compatibility, storage, bandwidth, convergence and abort checks; fencing; restore tests; and user-level readiness. The reserve question is whether remaining healthy capacity after one host or failure-domain loss can carry admitted demand plus hypervisor and recovery overhead within SLOs. Here 192 GiB requested exceeds 128 GiB raw, so the answer is no even before overhead.
foundation: KVM supplies a kernel execution interface, QEMU supplies machine and device emulation, and libvirt supplies stable management objects and drivers. None alone creates a private-cloud scheduler or HA policy. Desired domain XML, host/domain capabilities, actual QEMU process, guest state, storage chain, network path and user service are separate evidence layers. Running is not ready; migration completion is not correct recovery; multiple hosts are not independent failure domains.
reasoningSteps: Name the user operation and state that application readiness, identity and correctness are the outcome.
Separate host hardware and firmware, kernel KVM, QEMU, libvirt, domain definition, guest and application layers.
Inventory physical correlations: rack, power, management switch and writable storage.
Calculate fleet requests as 12 times 4 vCPU and 12 times 16 GiB.
Compare one-host survivor capacity to admitted demand before considering overcommit.
Reserve host memory for kernel, QEMU overhead, page cache, device emulation and recovery work.
Treat logical CPU count as a scheduling input, not a guarantee of workload throughput.
Bind host architecture, CPU features, NUMA and KVM capabilities.
Bind QEMU binary/version, machine type and CPU model instead of floating defaults.
Validate domain XML against schema and compare desired with effective runtime state.
Require unique domain name, UUID, MAC, firmware variables and storage ownership.
Declare disk formats rather than probing untrusted content.
Verify every qcow2 backing path, identity, hash or controlled image version and access permission.
Prevent two guests from writing one disk or writable NVRAM file.
Sanitize machine-id, SSH host keys, logs, leases and cloud-init cache before sealing a template.
Provide fresh per-instance datasource identity and metadata.
Trace bridge, tap, forwarding, DHCP/DNS, MAC/IP and policy for the migrated interface.
Replace unrestricted root with a least-privilege libvirt management role.
Encrypt and authenticate remote management and migration channels.
Preflight source and destination domain capabilities, CPU baseline and machine compatibility.
Preflight destination storage identity, allocation, free-space ceiling and permissions.
Measure migration bandwidth, dirty rate, convergence, downtime and application tolerance.
Define cancel or rollback behavior before migration and observe whether source or destination is authoritative.
Use fencing or leases to prevent two hosts or domain instances from controlling shared writable state.
Treat command completion as a narrow orchestration signal.
Validate guest boot stages, filesystem, identity, network and cloud-init result.
Validate the application and user path separately from VM running state.
Stop further migrations when identity, capacity, compatibility or storage safety is ambiguous.
Preserve source and destination logs, domain XML, capabilities, image-chain metadata and audit events.
Choose one authoritative instance and prevent duplicate network or storage effects.
Restore on a compatible host from a verified chain when safe in-place recovery is not possible.
Prove cleanup of duplicate identities, stale domain definitions, overlays, NVRAM and temporary migration artifacts.
Redesign placement across real rack, power, network and storage failure domains.
Define admission and reserve policy for one-host or one-domain loss plus recovery overhead.
Test backup restore independently because snapshots and shared storage are not backups.
State that the exercise proves only the exact topology, version, workload and evidence window.
seniorAnswer: I would declare the migration unsafe and the service unrecovered. Two hosts share rack, power, management and storage, and the fleet asks for 48 vCPU and 192 GiB; one 32-CPU/128-GiB host cannot carry the memory request after a host loss even before overhead. Floating CPU/machine identity, an unverified qcow2 chain, duplicate UUID/MAC/NVRAM/guest identity, plaintext root control and near-full destination storage invalidate preflight. I stop new operations, isolate duplicates, preserve exact source/destination/domain/image evidence, establish one authoritative writer, recover on a compatible host with verified capacity and chain, then validate guest identity, networking, cloud-init, application and user flow. The redesign binds capabilities and versions, unique identities, sanitized templates, image lineage, encrypted least privilege, real failure-domain placement, reserve/admission, migration convergence and abort, fencing, restore proof and service readiness. HA means a named service survives a named failure within measured bounds; host count alone proves nothing.
weakAnswer: The migration failed because the target CPU was older. Enable CPU passthrough, add disk space, restart the VM and configure both hosts as an HA cluster.
whyWeak: It misses physical and shared-storage correlation, impossible survivor memory capacity, floating compatibility, broken image lineage, duplicated VM/firmware/network/guest identity, unsafe control access, cloud-init semantics, fencing, application readiness, restore proof and the difference between a cluster label and measured recovery.

evidence.doesNotProve: Firmware enablement, kernel KVM support, /dev/kvm access or a compatible VM

evidence.proves: The caller can reach covered KVM kernel interfaces on that host
evidence.doesNotProve: QEMU, libvirt, domain, storage, network or guest readiness

evidence.proves: The reported driver/host and requested emulator-machine combination expose covered features
evidence.doesNotProve: A floating future host or runtime workload will be safe

evidence.signal: Validated domain XML and unique identities
evidence.proves: The desired definition satisfies covered schema and inventory rules

evidence.signal: qemu-img chain inspection and controlled image manifest
evidence.proves: The observed overlay lineage and image identity are complete within coverage
The management operation reached its completion state
evidence.doesNotProve: Single-writer authority, correct guest identity, network convergence or service readiness

evidence.signal: Independent user-path and state validation after soak
evidence.proves: The named service and invariants worked during the observed window
evidence.doesNotProve: Every failure domain, future version or workload

followUps.prompt: Why is host-passthrough risky for migration?
followUps.answer: It can expose source-specific CPU features that the destination lacks. A migration baseline must be compatible across the intended host pool and tested with the exact machine and emulator versions.

followUps.prompt: Why is a qcow2 snapshot not automatically a backup?
followUps.answer: An overlay depends on its backing chain and often shares the same storage, permissions and failure domain. Backup requires independently retained, identified and tested recoverable state.

followUps.prompt: What is the first reserve calculation here?
followUps.answer: Compare admitted guest memory plus host and recovery overhead with the capacity remaining after the declared failure. The requested 192 GiB already exceeds one survivor's raw 128 GiB.
Not Running alone. Prove correct domain and guest identity, disk/filesystem state, network path, initialization, application invariants and the named user operation over a soak window.
